title: Cellular automata cannot emulate substitution systems step for step

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Cellular automata cannot emulate substitution systems step for step

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Unlike mobile automata or Turing machines, substitution systems cannot in general be emulated one step per cellular automaton step, because the number of elements in a substitution system can be multiplied by a factor each step while a cellular automaton pattern can grow only by a fixed amount per step; progressively more cellular automaton steps are needed per substitution step.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: That this must ultimately be the case one can see from the fact that the total number of elements in a substitution system can be multiplied by a factor from one step to the next, while in a cellular automaton the size of a pattern can only ever increase by a fixed amount at each step.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 11, “The Notion of Computation”; section “Emulating Other Systems with Cellular Automata” (from p. 656), p. 658. Scope: cellular automaton emulation of substitution systems

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch11-08: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.90

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The growth-rate argument is finite and mathematically checkable. It cleanly resolves the intended direct emulation, though an unrestricted notion of encoding would need sharper assumptions.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare represented configuration length after t steps under a fixed-radius cellular automaton with a substitution system having multiplicative length growth. A linear light-cone bound rules out a length-preserving one-CA-step-per-substitution-step spatial encoding of the stated kind.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value: The impossibility depends on the intended local spatial encoding; highly compressed encodings require separate treatment.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The argument is a counting proof and applies to every cellular automaton, because every fixed radius grows by a bounded amount per step. It can be written in a page and illustrated by running any expanding substitution system beside any cellular automaton. The claim is exactly this general impossibility, which the inequality settles.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare growth rates. A substitution step may multiply the number of elements by a constant greater than one, while one step of a cellular automaton of radius r adds at most a fixed number of cells. Lockstep emulation is refuted by this inequality for expanding systems, and would be confirmed only by a construction that updates every substitution step in one cellular-automaton step for every such system.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value: The bound forbids one-step-per-step emulation of expanding systems; it says nothing against emulations that use increasingly many cellular-automaton steps.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

data adequacy: 0.95
data existence: 0.9

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: A one-dimensional cellular automaton of radius r can enlarge the region of non-background cells by at most 2r cells per step (light-cone bound), whereas a neighbour-independent substitution system can multiply its number of elements by a constant factor lambda > 1 per step. Hence for every substitution system with lambda > 1, any emulation in which each element occupies at least one cell needs a number of cellular-automaton steps per substitution step that grows without bound (at least (L_t - L_{t-1})/2r for step t), while Turing machines can be emulated one step per cellular-automaton step.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py: (A) evolves every quiescent elementary rule (128) from 10 random 20-cell seeds for 300 steps and 50 random quiescent radius-2 rules from 5 seeds for 200 steps on zero-padded lattices, recording the largest one-step increase of the non-zero region's width; (B) enumerates the 225 two-colour substitution systems with blocks of length 0-3, iterates each 12 times from a single black cell, compares the lengths with the growth-matrix prediction and computes the Perron root; (C) for growing systems computes the minimal number of radius-1 CA steps needed to accommodate the length, ceil((L_t - L_s)/2), over the whole run and over early and late windows; (D) builds, for 20 random 2-colour Turing machines, the radius-1 CA on 2(m+1) colours whose table is generated mechanically from the machine's rule, and compares the CA configuration with the machine's tape and head after each of 200 steps.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. (A) Light-cone bound: for all 128 elementary rules with quiescent background (000 -> 0), 10 random finite seeds of 20 cells each, 300 steps on a lattice wide enough never to reach the edge, the width of the non-zero region (rightmost minus leftmost black cell plus one) never increases by more than 2 in one step; likewise never by more than 4 for 50 random radius-2 two-colour rules with quiescent background (seeds 0-49), 5 seeds each, 200 steps. (B) Multiplicative growth: among all 225 two-colour neighbour-independent substitution systems with blocks of length 0-3, at least 50% have Perron root lambda > 1 of their 2x2 growth matrix, and for every system the lengths L_t for t <= 12 from a single black cell equal the matrix prediction exactly. (C) Growing cost: for every system with lambda > 1, the number of radius-1 cellular-automaton steps needed to contain L_12 cells starting from L_0 = 1, ceil((L_12 - L_0)/2), exceeds 12 (more than one CA step per substitution step on average), and the per-step requirement c_t = ceil((L_t - L_{t-1})/2) at t = 12 is at least 4 times c_t at t = 4 (progressively more steps). (D) Contrast with Turing machines: a radius-1 cellular automaton with k(s+1) colours (cell = tape colour x {no head, head state}) built mechanically from the Turing-machine rule reproduces the tape and head of 20 random 2-colour, 2-4-state Turing machines exactly at every one of 200 steps. 'Supports' requires A-D.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. 'Refutes' if A is violated for any rule, seed and step (the fixed-growth premise is false), or if any system with lambda > 1 has ceil((L_12 - L_0)/2) <= 12 (one CA step per substitution step is not excluded by the bound), or if D fails for any machine (Turing machines cannot be emulated step for step either, so the contrast is false). Other combinations are 'mixed'.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: minimum over growing substitution systems of radius-1 CA steps needed to hold 12 substitution steps of growth (threshold 12)

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: The claim is a counting argument. Its premise (fixed growth per CA step) is checked exhaustively over the elementary rules and on random larger-radius rules; the second premise (multiplicative growth of substitution systems) is checked over the complete family of two-colour systems with blocks of length 0-3 (NKS p. 82-83 convention: every element is replaced by the block for its colour; an empty block deletes the element); the conclusion is quantified as the minimal number of CA steps per substitution step under the only assumption that each element occupies at least one cell of the pattern (the encoding Wolfram's figures use; a compressed encoding would fall outside the claim's 'size of a pattern' reasoning). The clause 'unlike ... Turing machines' is checked by an explicit one-step-per-step construction (NKS p. 657). Computational; all programs generated by analysis.py.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: Elementary and radius-2 cellular automata, two-colour substitution systems, random Turing machines (generated by analysis.py)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Pre-registered criterion C failed for 12 of the 188 systems with Perron root > 1, and the pre-registered refutation trigger fired, so analysis.py reports preregistered_verdict = 'refutes'. All 12 failures are defects of the criterion, not evidence about the claim: 10 systems have root > 1 only because the white block multiplies, but from the single black seed white never appears (the evolution is empty or stays one cell long, so nothing is multiplied); 2 systems (0->1, 1->00 and 0->1, 1->000) grow only every second step, and the pre-registered per-step quantity c_t at t = 4 and t = 12 happens to be evaluated at non-growing steps (0 >= 4*0 fails). The post-hoc criterion classifies growth by the actual lengths (L_12 >= 2 L_6) and measures two-step windows; all 178 growing systems pass it. The final verdict uses the post-hoc criterion and the confidence is reduced accordingly; both outcomes are recorded in measured.extra.

The light-cone bound was checked empirically on finite families (all quiescent elementary rules, 50 random radius-2 rules); it is of course a theorem for any CA, and the empirical check found the bound attained (increase 2 per step) by 32 elementary rules.

Rules with 000 -> 1 (non-quiescent background) were excluded from A because 'size of a pattern' needs a fixed background; the bound applies to them relative to the alternating background but was not measured.

The impossibility concerns encodings in which each substitution element occupies at least one cell. Encodings that compress the configuration (e.g. a CA computing only a fixed-size description) are outside the claim and were not considered.

Random Turing machines in D have no halting state; the step-for-step CA construction (NKS p. 657) is the standard one and is verified only on 20 machines for 200 steps.
